title: Find a professional to certify export health certificates
text:
Guidance
Find a professional to certify export health certificates
A list of organisations in England, Scotland and Wales that inspect and certify animals and animal products for export. The list does not include every certifier.
From:
Animal and Plant Health Agency
Published:
8 February 2019
Last updated:
28 August 2026
          —
See all updates
Get emails about this page
Applies to England, Scotland and Wales
Documents
England: professionals who can certify export health certificates
HTML
Scotland: professionals who can certify export health certificates
HTML
Wales: professionals who can certify export health certificates
HTML
Details
The list only includes organisations who have asked to be included, so not every certifier in England, Scotland and Wales is listed.
If you want to export animals and animal products from the UK, you need to make sure someone signs an
export health certificate (
EHC
)
for your type of consignment.
This will be an Official Veterinarian (OV) or a local authority Food Competent Certifying Officer (FCCO). They will check that your consignment meets the health requirements of the destination country.
You can use this list to help you find an organisation that has certifiers permitted to certify your consignment. Not every certifier will be able to certify every consignment.
You must also check with them that they are registered to use
EHC
Online
. They will not be able to issue most certificates until they have registered.
There’s no fee for the certificate but you will usually be charged for the certifier’s time.
If your organisation offers export certification and you want it to be added to the list, email
CSCOneHealthOVTeam@apha.gov.uk
.
If you are in Northern Ireland, contact
DAERA
.

title: UK Shared Prosperity Fund: intervention-level evaluation
text:
August 2026 
Ministry of Housing, Communities & Local Government 
UK Shared Prosperity Fund: Intervention-
level Evaluation 
Support for People & Skills 
FINAL REPORT 

 
 
Contents 
Executive Summary 
i

1 
Chapter 2: Key findings 
10 
Chapter 3: Process evaluation findings on design and delivery 
40 
Chapter 4: Implications and lessons 
42 
 
 

 
i 
 
Executive Summary 
About this evaluation 
This report presents findings from the intervention-level evaluation of selected UK Shared 
Prosperity Fund (UKSPF) People & Skills projects. The report was prepared by Frontier 
Economics and BMG Research for the Ministry of Housing, Communities & Local 
Government (MHCLG). The findings are intended to support policy makers and local 
authorities in decisions on future funding and programme design. Technical details are 
provided in the annex (see ‘UKSPF intervention-level evaluation final technical annex: 
support for people and skills’). 
Local areas used UKSPF funding to support economically inactive people (defined as 
working aged people who are not working, actively seeking employment or in education or 
training) to move closer to, and into, employment. The nine projects in this evaluation 
provided £30 million of support to around 8,000 economically inactive participants 
across the UK. Each locally designed and delivered project delivered a combination of 
support activities to between 110 and 2,250 people. 
Support usually began with a one-to-one diagnostic consultation with an advisor or 
mentor, to identify participants’ needs and barriers. Projects then tailored support, 
including training, qualifications, coaching, mentoring and referrals to external services. 
The evaluation pooled participant data into a single dataset after distinctions between 
projects and their objectives became less clear. Participants were analysed by barriers to 
employment, soft skills, education and personal characteristics, enabling clearer 
assessment of what worked for different groups. 
The concept of “distance travelled” towards employment was central to the 
evaluation. This recognises that participants start from different positions and that progress 
towards work can take several forms including employment, qualifications, improved soft 
skills, reduced barriers and greater readiness for work.  
A key focus was to understand the link between soft skills and movement towards 
employment. This evaluation used a novel approach to measure perceived improvements 
in soft skills, and their correlation with employment outcomes. It also examined what 
support was delivered, who it reached, what outcomes were achieved and to what extent 
the support plausibly contributed to those outcomes. 
A contribution analysis evaluation approach was used, underpinned by a theory of change.  
Seven contribution claims were tested using monitoring data, qualitative evidence and 
survey responses from 799 participants who received support. 
For each claim, the analysis considered changes in outcomes, participants’ own 
assessment of the influence of the support, evidence on how the support led to change, 
and other factors that could also explain the outcomes. As no counterfactual group was 
available, the approach assessed whether the support plausibly contributed to the 
outcomes rather than establishing causality. 

 
ii 
 
Evidence strength for each contribution claim was assessed using a structured framework 
(see ‘UKSPF intervention-level evaluation final technical annex: support for people and 
skills’). This considered the quality, volume and consistency of evidence, and the extent to 
which alternative explanations could be ruled out. Findings were classified high-, medium- 
or low-strength. All findings included in this report are rated as either “high-strength” 
or “medium-strength”, meaning that it is at least reasonably clear that the support 
contributed to the outcomes.   
The evidence captures short-term outcomes only, usually around a month after UKSPF 
support ended for each participant. Longer-term outcomes may not yet have emerged. 
The findings are based on selected projects and should not be read as representative of 
the whole UKSPF People & Skills programme but provide an initial evidence base that can 
be tested and expanded over time.  
Key findings

Medium 
 
High-strength evidence shows that the support contributed to participants moving 
closer to, and into, employment. 
Across all projects, personalised one-to-one support helped individuals move into 
employment or closer to work. Within around one month of support ending: 
• 35% of participants had entered employment; and 
• A further 53% had made progress towards employment, for example by gaining 
qualifications, receiving job offers or improving soft skills.  
Together this means that around 90% of participants reduced their distance from the 
labour market. This is notable given that support targeted economically inactive people, 

 
iii 
 
who are often further from work than participants in other employment support 
programmes. 
Medium-strength evidence from qualitative sources shows that support contributed 
to improvements in wellbeing across all types of participants. For some participants, 
wellbeing improvement was an outcome in its own right. For others, it was also an enabler 
of progress towards employment or training. Quantitative evidence on wellbeing was not 
available for analysis because, when the survey was designed, wellbeing was not 
identified as a priority outcome and the limited survey space was instead used to measure 
soft skills, barriers, perceptions of support and employability outcomes. 
Outcomes varied depending on participants’ starting points, including their soft skills, time 
spent economically inactive and the nature of the barriers to employment they faced. 
Medium-strength evidence shows that support contributed to:  
• Recently inactive participants overcoming personal barriers to employment, 
moving into active job search and securing employment. Reported barriers 
reduced by 38%, from 2.0 barriers before support to 1.3 after support on average. 
Half (50%) of recently inactive individuals moved into employment or active job 
search after support: 32% secured employment and 18% were actively seeking 
work or had a job offer. 
• Long-term inactive participants overcoming personal barriers to employment, 
moving into active job search and securing employment. Reported barriers 
reduced from 2.2 barriers before support to 1.6 after support on average: a 27% 
reduction. Over half (57%) of long-term inactive individuals moved into employment 
or active job search after support. This included 31% who secured employment and 
26% who were actively seeking work or had a job offer. This was similar to the 
recently inactive cohort, despite a higher level of starting barriers. 
• The re-engagement of disengaged young participants with the education 
system. Around four-fifths (79%) of young people gained qualifications, while 
almost a quarter (24%) moved into employment. 
Participants who addressed barriers and improved soft skills were more likely to progress 
towards employment. 
How support contributed to change 
Addressing barriers was important: across all participants, barriers reduced by 38% on 
average. Barriers were reduced through confidence-building, practical employability 
support, and signposting or advocacy with wider services.  
Those who no longer reported barriers were more likely to enter employment than those 
whose barriers persisted. This link between reducing barriers and moving into employment 
was seen for those starting with high levels of barriers, not just those with low starting 
levels of barriers. Further, not all barriers needed to be removed to progress towards 
employment.  
Improving soft skills was a key outcome, often facilitated through reducing barriers. 
Eighty-five per cent of recently inactive participants and 72% of longer-term inactive 
participants said the support had helped at least one soft skill.  

 
iv 
 
Improving soft skills was a route to moving into employment. Participants who had 
improved their soft skills were more likely to move into employment: a one-point increase 
in soft skills was statistically significantly associated with a 6% higher likelihood of moving 
into employment. These skills increases mattered because they affected whether 
participants felt able to attend appointments, engage with training, contact employers, 
apply for jobs or follow through on referrals. 
Delivery models based on trusted relationships between advisors and participants, 
combined with the flexibility to tailor support, were central to achieving these 
outcomes. Advisors were able to exercise judgement over the intensity, sequencing and 
type of support provided. Flexible budgets for advisors also helped address practical 
barriers, such as transport.  
This flexibility enabled projects to reach participants in accessible ways, including through 
meetings in community settings rather than formal or centralised locations. Strong local 
partnerships with specialist providers also helped projects address a wide range of barriers 
in a coordinated way. 
For many participants, particularly those with more complex needs, progress involved 
stabilising their circumstances before employment or training became realistic. This 
included addressing issues such as mental health, housing or financial challenges, 
alongside building skills and confidence.  
Types of outcomes varied across different groups 
The types of outcomes achieved varied across participant groups. Participants closer 
to the labour market, such as those with higher initial skill levels or shorter periods of 
economic inactivity, were more likely to move directly into jobs. Younger participants and 
those further from the labour market were more likely to progress by gaining qualifications, 
entering education, improving skills or increasing their readiness for work.  
Support was effective for a wide range of individuals, including those with complex 
needs. Participants with lower starting skill levels or more complex barriers often 
experienced some of the largest improvements in soft skills and reductions in barriers, 
even where this did not translate into immediate employment within the evaluation period.  
Wellbeing improvements were also widely reported in qualitative evidence. These 
were both a direct benefit of support and, for many participants, an important enabler of 
engagement with employability activities and future labour market progression. 
This reinforces that progress is not expected to be uniform across participants and 
success should be judged both by employment outcomes and by credible progress 
towards work, particularly for participants starting further from the labour market. 
Delivering value for money 
Overall, the findings suggest that UKSPF-funded personalised support for 
economically inactive individuals can deliver positive outcomes and represent 
medium value for money, even within a relatively short timeframe. The evidence 
indicates that these outcomes were associated with relatively intensive, tailored forms of 
support.  

 
v 
 
Value for money was assessed using methods appropriate to each type of intervention 
over a five-year period by comparing project costs with observable benefits, consistent 
with relevant sector best practice, HM Treasury Green Book guidance and MHCLG value 
for money categories. 1, 2 Given differences in methods and evidence, estimates should not 
be interpreted as directly comparable across interventions. 
Employment and wellbeing benefits were monetised where possible and non-monetised 
benefits were also considered.  
These findings should be interpreted cautiously. The analysis reflects short-term 
outcomes, excluding some wider benefits that could not be robustly monetised, and 
remains uncertain given the limited time since project completion. Further evidence would 
be needed to confirm whether these benefits are sustained over time.  
Continuity of provision and the retention of experienced delivery staff were identified as 
important enablers of effective delivery. This suggests that stable funding and delivery 
arrangements can help maintain the advisor skills, local relationships and flexible support 
models associated with positive outcomes.  
Implications for policy makers 
Key findings include:  
• Protect trusted one-to-one advisor relationships. The evidence consistently 
points to trusted relationships between participants and advisors as a central 
feature associated with positive outcomes. Delivery models that allowed advisors to 
build sustained relationships, exercise judgement, tailor support and signpost to 
other services appear to have underpinned effectiveness.  
• Maintain flexibility to address practical barriers. Funding flexibility, including the 
ability of advisors to use budgets to address practical barriers such as transport, 
was regarded as key to success. Local partnerships with specialist providers were 
also important, enabling projects to address a wide range of barriers to employment 
in a coordinated way.  
• Support continuity in funding and delivery. Longer funding periods would 
support continuity of provision and help retain experienced delivery staff. These 
staff skills, relationships and local knowledge were seen as important for effective 
delivery. 
• Recognise that personalised support can offer value for money. Supporting 
economically inactive individuals with a range of needs can be done in a 
personalised way while offering value for money. Even under conservative 
assumptions and within a short observation window, the monetised benefits are 
expected to exceed costs, with additional benefits likely to emerge over time.  
• Value and monitor progress towards work, not only job entry. Programmes of 
this type would not be expected to move all participants into employment within a 
short period. Future programmes should track intermediate outcomes such as 
 
 
1 The Green Book - GOV.UK  
2 The MHCLG Appraisal Guide - GOV.UK 

 
vi 
 
reduced barriers, improved soft skills, qualifications and wellbeing, as these can be 
meaningful steps toward future employment.

 
1 
 
Chapter 1: Introduction and methodology 
1.1: Policy context and purpose of this report 
The UK Shared Prosperity Fund (UKSPF) provided £3.5 billion of funding for local 
investment between 2022 and 2026, with the aim of supporting growth and promoting 
opportunities across all parts of the UK. 
Local authorities had significant flexibility in how they spent UKSPF funding. This helped 
them to design projects to meet local needs. Projects varied in their scale, design and who 
they supported. In this report, a “project” refers to a locally designed and delivered 
programme of UKSPF-funded support for economically inactive local people. 
This report presents findings from the intervention‑level evaluation of selected UKSPF 
People & Skills projects that support economically inactive people to get closer to work. It 
focuses on: 
• how projects were delivered (process evaluation); 
• what outcomes were achieved and whether these plausibly reflect UKSPF 
contribution (impact evaluation); and 
• whether benefits are likely to outweigh costs (value for money evaluation). 
Findings are presented by study group and are not intended to be representative of the 
whole UKSPF programme.  
1.2: The revised study group approach 
It was not proportionate to evaluate all UKSPF interventions under the People & Skills 
theme across the UK. To manage diversity and generate transferable learning, the 
evaluation took a two-stage approach. First, it identified some groups of similar 
interventions, based on having shared objectives, target participants and delivery models, 
and allocated them to potential “study groups”. Three study groups were selected for 
evaluation based on feasibility, policy interest, coverage of different contexts and 
proportionate evaluation. 
Projects within each study group were then selected according to criteria that ensured they 
were varied in size (UKSPF funding), scale (geographical coverage), UK nation, types of 
support provided, and their ability to address gaps in the evidence on the effectiveness of 
similar local interventions. 
All study groups selected wanted to improve soft outcomes for inactive individuals but 
intended to target different groups within the inactive population. As the evaluation and 
understanding of the projects evolved, it became clear that the distinction between the study 
groups was increasingly blurred. Projects in fact targeted wide groups of people covering a 
spectrum of distances from employment.  

 
2 
 
Rather than sticking rigidly to the study group approach, data from across the study groups 
was pooled together to provide a single large dataset. This meant that the evaluation could 
explore what worked for different groups of participants. Grouping was done according to 
type of perceived personal barriers to employment, level of soft skills, existing education and 
personal characteristics. This was instead of grouping by study group, which would have 
been less precise. 
This approach supports clear lessons on what works, for whom and under what conditions, 
and complements the UKSPF place-based evaluation, which examines how combinations 
of interventions work within different types of places and alongside other local growth 
funding. 
Further information on the selection of the study groups is available in the Feasibility 
Report and the approach to pooling project data in the Early Update Report.  
1.3: Overview of the interventions 
The evaluation collected evidence from nine UKSPF-funded projects within the People & 
Skills theme, across three study groups.  
The study groups were originally selected to cover three distinct types of projects, aimed at 
capturing various potential distances from employment:  
• Those which targeted young people who were hard to reach and far from 
employment;  
• Those which targeted a broad range of people with different distances to 
employment; and  
• Those which targeted people who were perceived to be closer to employment when 
starting the support. These people were considered to be closer to employment 
than other inactive individuals but not necessarily “close” to employment. 
Together, these projects supported around 8,000 economically inactive people, with 
targeted participants ranging from 110 to 2,250 per project. The survey sample (799) is 
smaller than the total number of participants supported but it includes participants from all 
study groups. It captures a broad range of participants across these projects. 
These are all large projects: funding for delivering them from 2022 to 2025 ranged from 
£0.9 to £7.5 million per project. Most projects involved multiple delivery partners, with over 
20 organisations involved in these nine projects. There is substantial variation in the size 
of the projects (by funding and participant numbers). Bias in the findings was minimised by 
the analysis focusing on individuals rather than projects and the triangulation across data 
sources to avoid over-reliance on a single source. 
The projects all used multiple recruitment methods for participants, combining Jobcentre 
Plus referrals with referrals from health providers and local voluntary and community 
organisations and bespoke community outreach. Self-referral was also permitted for all of 
the projects. Participation was voluntary for all projects. 
The projects were drawn from across the UK, reflecting a range of local contexts. 

 
3 
 
• England: Liverpool City Region and Durham; 
• Wales: Cardiff and Blaenau Gwent; 
• Scotland: Fife; and 
• Northern Ireland: One project is Northern Ireland-wide, a second focuses on 
Belfast, and a third covers Newry, Mourne & Down and Armagh City, Banbridge & 
Craigavon Councils. 
1.3.1: Reducing the distance to employment 
Filling the evidence gap on the links between improvements in some “soft” outcomes for 
inactive individuals and movements towards and into employment was a particular focus of 
the evaluation. This evaluation provides new and valuable evidence with a novel approach 
to directly measure perceived soft skill improvements and their correlation with 
employment outcomes.  
The concept of “distance travelled” towards employment was key. It was used to measure 
improvements in “soft outcomes” that are consistent with a movement towards “hard 
outcomes” such as employment or education.3 This evaluation defines soft outcomes as 
improved soft skills (like confidence and job search skills) or the removal of perceived 
barriers to employment. This is grounded in existing evidence and developed with the 
theories of change for the projects (see ‘UKSPF intervention-level evaluation final 
technical annex: support for people and skills’). 
The starting distance to employment varies for every inactive individual due to the unique 
combination of barriers to employment they face and their initial soft skills, education and 
qualification levels. Projects did not anticipate that all individuals, regardless of starting 
position, would be able to move into employment from the intervention. This means that 
what is needed to move a participant closer to employment is a function of the starting 
place. Figure 1 shows this.

1.3.2: Support was tailored to the individual 
All projects offered broadly similar approaches to identifying and providing the support that 
individual participants needed. They all included an initial assessment stage where the 
individual’s current skills and barriers were identified, with a bespoke programme of 
support being designed for the individual following this assessment. Projects could offer 
tailored support and training from a long list of options, from formal training that resulted in 
qualifications to informal coaching and mentoring.  
All projects included some form of one-to-one support and were able to adjust the 
frequency and nature of this support to respond to the individual’s needs and specific 
circumstances. In most cases, the length of time support was provided for varied by 
participant, although the majority of support lasted between 3 and 12 months. All projects 
also signposted participants to other specialist support organisations where necessary, 
with delivery staff acting as connectors and advocates. 
1.4: Evaluation approach 
The evaluation questions focus on what works, for whom and under what 
conditions, including the conditions for delivering value for money. For detail on the 
approach, see ‘UKSPF intervention-level evaluation final technical annex: support for 
people and skills’. 
 

 
5 
 
1.4.1: Evaluation framework and contribution analysis 
The evaluation was designed around a theory-based framework, underpinned by theories 
of change for each study group (see ‘UKSPF intervention-level evaluation final technical 
annex: support for people and skills’). These set out how UKSPF-funded support was 
intended to lead to economically inactive people moving closer to and into employment.  
Given the localised project delivery and the infeasibility of sufficient quasi-experimental 
designs within this evaluation period, the evaluation used contribution analysis as its 
primary impact approach. Contribution analysis is recognised in HM Treasury’s Magenta 
Book as a robust method for assessing whether, how and why an intervention has 
plausibly contributed to the observed outcomes, particularly in complex settings where 
controlled comparisons are not feasible.4 
The contribution analysis approach involved developing a set of contribution claims, which 
defined how support was expected to influence employment outcomes, and provided a 
structured basis for testing whether the expected pathways set out in the theory of change 
were supported in practice. 
The evaluation tested these claims using a combination of quantitative evidence (including 
survey data on changes in outcomes and self-reported attribution) and qualitative evidence 
(from interviews and focus groups) to assess how and why outcomes occurred. Qualitative 
evidence was also used separately as part of the process evaluation to understand how 
support was delivered and experienced. 
The analysis used econometric techniques to explore how outcomes varied across 
different participant groups. This allowed an understanding of the relative effectiveness of 
this type of support for delivering different outcomes for different groups. 
For further information on the approach design, see the Feasibility Report.  
1.4.2: Contribution claims tested 
Across the pooled dataset of participants, seven contribution claims were developed, 
reflecting the key pathways to impact set out in the theory of change (see ‘UKSPF 
intervention-level evaluation final technical annex: support for people and skills’):  
1. UKSPF support helped recently inactive people to overcome personal barriers to 
employment. 
2. UKSPF support contributed to recently inactive people moving into active job 
search and securing employment. 
3. UKSPF support helped long-term inactive people to overcome practical personal 
barriers to employment. 
4. UKSPF support contributed to long-term inactive people moving into active job 
search and securing employment.

5. UKSPF support contributed to the re-engagement of disengaged young people with 
the education system.    
6. UKSPF support contributed to participants moving closer to and into employment 
across all cohorts. 
7. UKSPF support contributed to improvements in wellbeing across all participant 
groups. 
Contribution claims 1-5 group participants by different distances from employment and the 
outcomes achieved. Distance from employment refers to how close a participant is to 
being ready and able to enter work, taking account of employment status, job search 
activity, qualifications, education, soft skills and reported barriers. Soft skills in this 
evaluation covered confidence, employability skills, job search skills and setting, and 
achieving goals. 
1.4.3: Data sources 
The evaluation drew on project monitoring data, surveys and qualitative evidence from 
interviews and focus groups: 
• Bespoke survey was administered to participants as a baseline at the start of their 
support and as an opt-in survey within around a month of completing support. A 
response rate of 20% for the follow-on survey provided data on 799 participants 
across all projects with before-and-after data. The dataset combined information on 
the starting characteristics and barriers to employment facing individuals with 
information on soft (confidence, readiness for work, etc.) and hard outcomes 
(employment, qualifications, job offer, etc.) before and after the projects.  
o Monitoring data were provided by most projects and was incorporated into 
the dataset with the survey data. This included employment outcomes 
captured by the project, which were compared with employment outcomes 
reported by the participants in the surveys 
• Qualitative evidence from semi-structured interviews with participants, delivery 
partners, frontline staff and local authorities provided additional insight into how 
support was delivered, experienced and perceived. Focus groups helped to 
contextualise the survey findings and understand how support contributed to 
outcomes in practice. 
• Contextual information, such as local labour market statistics on travel to work 
times and unemployment rates, was used to interpret and frame the findings. 
The data collection was designed to minimise burdens on participants, delivery staff and 
local authorities, recognising their limited time and capacity. 
1.4.4: Impact evaluation quantitative approach 
The survey data enabled before-and-after analysis by participant. 

 
7 
 
More robust econometric analysis explored how outcomes varied across different groups 
within the inactive population, including consideration of how outcomes varied by starting 
barriers, soft skills and personal characteristics. This allowed an understanding of the 
relative effectiveness of these projects for delivering different outcomes for different 
groups.  
The findings are considered robust as a result of the large sample size and because the 
characteristics of those in the follow-up survey were similar to those who only provided 
baseline data (see ‘UKSPF intervention-level evaluation final technical annex: support for 
people and skills’).  
The findings are likely to provide transferable learning for similar programmes given that 
they cover both a range of geographical settings and contexts and individuals sitting 
across the broad spectrum of distance to employment.  
1.4.5: Assessing the strength of evidence 
The strength of evidence for each of the seven contribution claims was assessed using a 
bespoke framework (see ‘UKSPF intervention-level evaluation final technical annex: 
support for people and skills’). Ratings reflect the quality, volume and consistency of 
evidence across sources, and the extent to which alternative explanations could account 
for the outcomes observed:  
• High-strength evidence means that the theory of change was validated, at least 
three different sources of evidence or analysis produced similar findings, almost all 
evidence pointed to the same conclusion, and other drivers were judged to have 
had only a minimal influence on the outcome. 
• Medium-strength evidence means that the theory of change was mostly validated, 
most evidence pointed to the same conclusion, and other drivers were likely to have 
influenced the outcome, but less so than the UKSPF support. 
• Low-strength evidence means that there was either an absence of sufficient 
evidence to draw a conclusion or that the theory of change could not be validated, 
evidence pointed to differing conclusions and other factors could have explained the 
outcomes.  
Each contribution claim was assessed as having high-, medium- or low-strength evidence, 
or as having insufficient evidence at this stage (see ‘UKSPF intervention-level evaluation 
final technical annex: support for people and skills’).  
1.4.6: Assessing value for money 
Value for money (VfM) is defined by HM Treasury as a balanced judgement about the 
optimal use of public resources to achieve intended outcomes. In this context, VfM is 
assessed using a framework consistent with the HM Treasury Green Book guidance, 
combining monetised benefits with wider non-monetisable outcomes.5 
The analysis monetised employment outcomes achieved within the timeframe of the 
evaluation, using wage benefits as the primary monetised benefit. It also considered the

potential value of intermediate outcomes, such as participants gaining qualifications, 
entering education or training, receiving job offers or actively looking for work, where these 
outcomes may lead to employment in the future. Wellbeing benefits associated with 
employment were also monetised separately. 
Estimates were based on impact evaluation findings, combined with conservative 
assumptions drawn from published literature and government guidance. Benefits were 
assessed over a five-year time horizon and discounted in line with Green Book guidance. 
Key assumptions, including the expected duration of employment benefits and the 
likelihood that intermediate outcomes lead to employment, were tested through sensitivity 
analysis. As no counterfactual was available, the analysis used attribution and deadweight 
assumptions to estimate the share of outcomes that could reasonably be linked to the 
support.  
The assessment of VfM used in this evaluation considered what level of benefits would be 
needed to outweigh the costs. This is because only some benefits were monetisable and 
the duration of benefits was also uncertain.  
VfM categories were defined based on monetised benefit-cost ratios (BCRs), in line with 
MHCLG guidance. A BCR of 1 to 1.5 represents acceptable value for money, rising to very 
high value for money at a BCR above 4.6 These categories reflect monetisable outcomes 
only and should be interpreted alongside wider benefits that cannot be monetised. For 
further details, see ‘UKSPF intervention-level evaluation final technical annex: support for 
people and skills’. 
1.5: Limitations for interpreting results  
There are key limitations to consider when interpreting the results:  
• Outcomes were observed around one month after participants finished support. The 
evaluation did not include a comparison group, so findings should be interpreted as 
contribution evidence rather than proof that all outcomes were caused by UKSPF 
support alone. However, the findings are consistent across survey evidence, 
econometric analysis, qualitative fieldwork and case-study evidence. 
• The one-month response period was chosen to maximise responses. This means 
that it is not possible to comment on either the longevity of observed outcomes or 
how longer-term outcomes might evolve within this evaluation.  
• The econometrics looked at the effectiveness of the projects at offering bespoke 
targeted support to individuals overall. It was not possible to analyse whether 
certain targeted activities offered within the projects worked well – for example, 
analysing the relative effectiveness of a work placement versus support in CV 
preparation across or within groups. It was not possible to systematically gather this 
data from local authorities. Even if it had been, it might still not have been possible 
to draw conclusions about the relative effectiveness of different activities given the 
highly varied starting positions of individuals.

Chapter 2: Key findings 
2.1: Summary of findings 
Across the People & Skills projects in this evaluation, UKSPF-funded support made 
a meaningful contribution to moving economically inactive participants closer to 
work. The strongest evidence is that participants reported fewer barriers, improved 
confidence and work-related skills, and moved into employment, active job search, 
education or qualifications. 
The pathway to change varied by starting point: 
• Recently inactive participants were more likely to convert support into immediate 
labour market activity.  
• Long-term inactive participants also moved into employment or active job search, 
but often while continuing to manage more persistent barriers.  
• Young people (under 25 years) in youth-focused projects were more likely to 
progress through education, qualifications and re-engagement, reflecting the design 
of those projects and the starting point of the participants they supported. 
Qualitative evidence reinforced the complexity of participants’ starting points. As one 
delivery partner explained: 
“You can’t put somebody in one box and say, this is their challenge, because they 
come with a plethora of challenges. And that takes quite a while sometimes to 
support somebody and provide a provision that is on one hand bespoke but can 
address groups of people.” (Delivery partner) 
These differences by starting point are explored in contribution claims 1 through 5. 
The barriers reported by participants included perceived, practical and labour 
market barriers. Changes in reported barriers may therefore reflect actual changes in 
circumstances, changes in participants’ ability to manage those barriers, or changes in 
how participants understood their options. For example, support could not directly change 
the type or number of jobs available locally, but it could help participants identify suitable 
roles, understand transferable skills, broaden the range of jobs they considered or manage 
practical constraints. The support intentionally aimed to change perceptions about the 
types of jobs appropriate for participants to apply to, even though the support could not 
change the actual jobs available. 
The evidence supports the effectiveness of the personalised support model overall. 
It does not allow the evaluation to isolate the impact of individual activities, such as CV 
support, interview preparation, training or work placements. The common support model 
combined assessment, trusted one-to-one support, tailored sequencing, practical help, 
local delivery and referrals to specialist services. 
Trusted relationships were central to this model. One delivery partner explained: 

 
11 
 
“All of the staff ... would talk about ... the building of the trust, which is so important, 
building trust with all of their participants and building a relationship with the 
participants, which takes time ... but in each of those areas, I think that has been 
really key to the delivery of ... the project.” (Delivery Partner) 
This matters for policy because it suggests that personalised employment support 
for economically inactive people should not be judged only by immediate 
employment outcomes. Employment is the clearest end outcome, but for participants 
further from work, reduced barriers, improved confidence, qualifications, education or 
active job search can be meaningful steps towards later employment. 
2.2: Contribution claim findings 
2.2.1: Contribution claim 1: UKSPF support helped recently inactive 
participants to overcome personal barriers to employment  
This claim relates to participants who had been out of work or full-time education for less 
than a year. This group made up 46% of survey respondents. It included many young 
people, who, by definition, could not have been out of work or education for long periods of 
time (58% of this group).  
Survey evidence shows that recently inactive participants reported fewer barriers to 
employment after receiving support. On average, the number of reported barriers 
fell from 2.0 before support to 1.3 after support, a reduction of 38%. The share that 
reported 5 or more barriers also fell from 9% to 4%.  
Among recently inactive participants who reported at least 1 barrier before support, 26% 
reported no barriers by the end of support. Among those that reported 5 or more barriers 
before support, 54% reported fewer than 5 after support.  
Reported reductions were seen across all barrier types. The most common starting 
barriers for this group were not having the right qualifications, the types of jobs available, 
the number of jobs available and access to transport as shown in Figure 2. The number of 
participants that reported each of these barriers fell after support. The largest reductions 
were in the number that reported that they did not have the right qualifications, did not 
have a permanent place to live, or had limited or no internet access. Each fell by just over 
50%.  
Some barriers remained. After support, 22% still reported not having the right 
qualifications as a barrier, 22% reported the type of jobs available as a barrier and 19% 
reported access to transport as a barrier. This means that the evidence indicates that 
support helped many recently inactive participants to address or manage barriers but did 
not remove all constraints for all participants within the evaluation period.

How support contributed to change

linked routes:  
1. confidence-building;  
2. practical employability support; and

their confidence and 77% said it had helped them set and achieve goals, as shown in

attend appointments, engage with training, contact employers, apply for jobs or follow

Second, support helped participants to develop employability and job search skills. 
Recently inactive participants had relatively low starting levels of job search skills, with an 
average self-rated score of 3.0 on a 6-point scale. After support, 74% reported that the 
programme had helped improve their job search skills and 77% reported that it had 
improved their employability skills. 
Third, support helped participants to access wider services. Advisors and delivery 
staff signposted participants to specialist provision, helped them understand available 
support and, in some cases, advocated on their behalf. This was particularly important 
where barriers were linked to housing, health, caring responsibilities or digital exclusion. 
External services therefore acted both as an additional influence on outcomes and as part 
of the route through which UKSPF support contributed to change. 
Qualitative evidence suggests this was more than simple signposting. As one delivery 
partner and local authority explained: 
“We will seek the supplier that’s the closest to that individual that’s accessible to 
them … it’s all about finding the provision that the individual needs that’s on their 
doorstep that they’re happy to engage with and then support them through that 
process … It’s not just about making a referral to Citizens Advice [for example] for 
someone, and then a week later go ‘how did you get on’ and finding out that they 
didn’t turn up … we hold their hand, we open the door, we show them through, we 
sit them down.” (Delivery partner) 
“We were able to pay them [Citizens Advice] to give us some specified dedicated 
staff time rather than saying to people ‘You really should get to Citizen’s Advice, it’s 
down the road and you’ll probably wait three weeks’. That fast tracking was really 
important.” (Local authority) 
The programmes appear to have helped participants through targeted support that 
addressed their needs in a range of ways depending on the barriers they faced. The

The type and intensity of support varied between participants. For some, the emphasis 
was on building confidence and motivation. For others, it focused more on employability 
skills, job search activity, qualifications, work experience, signposting or advocacy with 
wider services. 
These different forms of support were relevant to participants depending on their 
starting points and the barriers they faced. For example, improvements in confidence 
could make it easier for some participants to engage with training or job search activity, 
while practical support could help others see employment as more achievable. This 
tailored approach helps to explain why many participants reported fewer barriers to 
employment by the end of support.

beneficiaries get closer to employment. In both examples, the frequency and intensity of 
the support, including the one-to-one mentoring was matched to the beneficiary’s needs, 
as is typical for the projects.

Other factors influencing outcomes 
Other factors may also have reduced reported barriers. Participants’ personal 
circumstances may have changed, and some may have received informal or formal 
support outside the programme. The evaluation cannot fully rule out these explanations. 
However, the evidence suggests that UKSPF support made a distinct contribution. 
Delivery partners consistently reported that participants faced complex and connected 
barriers, and that signposting alone would not have been sufficient for many of them. Local 

 
16 
 
authorities and delivery partners also reported limited availability of comparable support in 
many areas. Participants consistently reported that the programme had helped them make 
progress. 
Taken together, the evidence does not show that UKSPF support was the only factor that 
influenced outcomes. It does suggest that other factors are unlikely to explain the full scale 
and pattern of barrier reduction observed. 
Overall assessment of contribution 
Medium-strength evidence suggests that personalised support contributed to reductions 
in reported barriers. This combines quantitative before-and-after survey data, self-reported 
impacts and qualitative evidence from local authorities, delivery partners and participants 
for how the personalised support enabled this. 
 
2.2.2: Contribution claim 2: UKSPF support contributed to recently inactive 
participants moving into active job search and securing employment 
The previous claim showed that recently inactive participants reported fewer barriers after 
support. This claim considers whether that progress translated into movement towards 
work through active job search, job offers or employment. 
Survey evidence shows that 50% of recently inactive participants moved into 
employment or active job search after support: 32% secured employment and 18% 
were actively seeking work or had a job offer. 
For an economically inactive cohort, active job search is a meaningful outcome. It 
represents a move towards the labour market and, for some participants, a change in 
labour market status. This outcome should therefore be interpreted as more than a 
measure of intention: it shows that some participants moved from inactivity into practical 
job search activity. 
This finding strengthens the contribution story from contribution claim 1. For many recently 
inactive participants, reduced reported barriers and improved soft skills were followed by 
active steps towards work.

How support contributed to change 
Support appears to have contributed in three ways:  
1. converting confidence and motivation into action;  
2. providing practical employability and job search support; and  
3. helping participants manage remaining barriers while moving towards work. 
Survey evidence shows that, among recently inactive participants who moved into 
employment or active job search, 85% reported that the programme had helped with 
at least one soft skill. These skills helped participants look for work, apply for jobs, present 
themselves to employers and maintain momentum through recruitment: 
• 77% reported that it helped with confidence. 
• 73% reported that it helped with setting and achieving goals.  
• 85% of those that reported low scores for these skills at the outset reported that 
support had helped improve their job search skills and employability.  
Support also helped participants develop practical skills directly linked to finding 
work. Among recently inactive participants who moved into active job search or 
employment, around 75% reported that support had helped improve their employability 
skills and job search skills. This included support with CVs, applications, interview 
preparation, vacancy searches and identifying suitable roles. 
Participants who moved into employment or active job search reported 
improvements in the skills most closely linked to labour market action, particularly 
confidence, goal setting, employability and job search skills. Among those with low 
starting scores, close to 90% improved in each soft skill area as shown in Figure 6, 
although this finding is based on a smaller sample and should be interpreted cautiously.

participants to overcome personal barriers to employment  
This claim relates to participants who had been out of work or education for more than a 
year. This group made up 36% of participants. Many were aged 24 or below, although 
young people made up a smaller share of this group than of the recently inactive group. 
Survey evidence shows that long-term inactive participants started further from 
employment than recently inactive participants on several measures. They reported 
an average of 2.2 barriers before support, compared with 2.0 among recently inactive 
participants. Twelve per cent reported 5 or more barriers before support. 
• After support, the average number of reported barriers fell from 2.2 to 1.6, a reduction 
of 27%.  
• The share who reported 5 or more barriers fell from 12% to 7%.  
• For those who reported at least 1 barrier before support, 13% reported no barriers 
after support.  
• For those who reported 5 or more barriers before support, 39% reported fewer than 
5 after support. 
These reductions were smaller than for recently inactive participants but still indicate 
progress for a group that started further from work. 

 
21 
 
Reported reductions were seen across most barrier types. The most common starting

2.2.5: Contribution claim 5: UKSPF support contributed to the re-engagement 
of disengaged young participants with the education system    
Young people were supported through both youth-focused projects and broader People & 
Skills projects. The youth-focused projects intentionally targeted hard-to-reach young 
people, many of whom had limited engagement with education and were further from 
employment than young people in broader provision. 
Lower short-term employment rates among young people in youth-focused projects should 
not be interpreted as weaker performance. These projects intentionally targeted young 
people further from work and placed greater emphasis on re-engagement, qualifications 
and education pathways. 
Survey evidence shows that young people in youth-focused projects were less likely to 
enter employment within the evaluation period than young people in broader projects. 
Twenty-four per cent of young people in youth-focused projects entered employment, 
compared with 44% of young people in broader projects. However, young people in youth-
focused projects were more likely to gain qualifications or move into education and 
training. 
Nearly 80% (79%) of young people in youth-focused projects gained a qualification, 
compared with 27% of young people in broader projects. The difference in employment 
outcomes does not appear to be explained only by starting education levels. Young people 
with Level 2 or higher starting qualifications in youth-focused projects were still less likely 
to enter employment than those with equivalent starting education in broader projects. 
This suggests that youth-focused projects were more oriented towards education and 
qualification outcomes in the short term. This is consistent with their purpose: to rebuild 
routine, confidence, skills and engagement with learning for young people who had 
become detached from education or work. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
29 
 
How support contributed to change 
The key route through which support contributed was the youth worker approach: flexible, 
relationship-based support that moved at the young person’s pace and addressed wider 
personal barriers before focusing narrowly on employment. 
One delivery partner described the early stages of their programme: 
“Phase one of the programme is all about personal development and wellbeing. We 
don’t mention qualifications, we don’t mention jobs, we don’t mention careers. That 
phase is on reducing the barriers of young people to engage in or build more trust 
… Phase one is run by our youth mentors who all come from a youth work 
background. They do a lot of team building, confidence, self-esteem. If they need 
referrals for additional support … anything around alcohol, drugs, childcare … 
relationship advisors … money, finance people, welfare rights people … They just 
do a lot of things that set them up and deal with the initial issues that have caused 
them to be economically inactive.” (Delivery partner) 
Youth-focused projects appear to have been particularly effective at improving soft skills 
for young people with low starting levels. This matters because, for disengaged young 
people, confidence, motivation, routine and goal setting are often necessary foundations 
for education, training or employment outcomes. 
Frontline staff described this as an intentional focus: 
“For me it’s education and skills outcomes. Skills development is the most 
important. And we’ve blasted that out of the sky.” (Frontline staff) 
The relationship between qualifications and employment/actively looking for 
employment 
Gaining a qualification is not a good predictor of moving into employment in this 
evaluation. Participants who gained a qualification were, in fact, less likely to be in 
employment than those who did not gain a qualification as part of the support. This 
relationship is stronger for participants who started with lower levels of soft skills and 
gained a qualification. That means that, when comparing two participants with lower 
levels of soft skills at the beginning of the project, the one who gained a qualification 
during the project was less likely to also be in employment compared to one who did 
not gain a qualification. 
A potential explanation is that these participants, having spent the duration of the 
project working towards that qualification, did not find a job within the survey timings, 
and that gaining qualifications may have been more important for participants starting 
with lower levels of soft skills. Another possible reason is that a large proportion of 
participants who gained a qualification were in the study group for hard-to-reach 
young people, which tended more to have education outcomes. 
Similarly, having gained a qualification did not affect the likelihood of actively looking 
for a job. The same explanations as above are relevant for this relationship. 

 
30 
 
Case-study evidence illustrates how this worked. For some young people with repeated 
disengagement from sixth form or college, caring responsibilities or mental health 
challenges, support focused first on trust, interests and strengths. This then enabled young 
people to explore education pathways, volunteering, qualifications or longer-term 
employment ambitions. 
Re-engagement with education should therefore be treated as a meaningful labour market 
outcome for young people who are not ready to move directly into work. It can also provide 
a route to better-quality and more sustainable employment later.

2.2.6: Contribution claim 6: UKSPF support contributed to participants 
moving closer to and into employment across all cohorts 
This claim brings together the evidence across all participants. It does not repeat the 
subgroup analysis above. Instead, it assesses whether the overall pattern of outcomes is 
consistent with the theory that personalised support helped participants reduce their 
distance from employment. 
Across all cohorts, 90% of participants reduced their distance from employment, 
measured by outcomes like employment, qualifications and increases in soft skills. 
Participants are counted once, according to their closest-to-employment outcome. This 
means, for example, that a participant who entered employment and also gained a 
qualification is counted under employment. It also means that an increase in soft skills is 
only counted by itself where the participant did not also, for example, gain a qualification. 
Across the whole sample, average soft skills increased for 40% of participants 
This pattern is consistent with the projects’ objectives. The projects supported 
economically inactive people with varied and often complex needs. They did not expect all 
participants to move directly into employment within the evaluation period. For many 
participants, progress towards work was expected to involve intermediate outcomes such 
as improved confidence, skills, qualifications, reduced barriers or active job search: 
• 35% moved into employment.7 
• 53% moved closer to employment. Of these, in order of closest to employment: 
o 8% had a job offer 
o 34% were actively looking for work 
o 44% gained a qualification 
o 11% were in full-time or part-time education 
o 3% improved their average level of soft skills to reduce their expected 
distance to employment without any additional outcomes above.  
 
 
7 Many of these participants will have also increased their soft skills 

 
33 
 
• A further 2% reported a reduction in their number of barriers, with no other positive 
outcomes. And for half of them, barriers reduced even while the average skill levels 
reported decreased compared to reported levels before the support. 
• 10% experienced no apparent reduction in the distance to employment from the 
above outcomes or a reduction in barriers.8  
How support contributed to change (delivery model set out in earlier section) 
Across all cohorts, the evidence suggests that personalised support reduced 
distance from employment through two main routes: reducing barriers and 
improving soft skills (confidence, employability and job search skills). 
First, support contributed to reductions in reported barriers:  
• Across all participants, the average number of reported barriers fell from 2.0 before 
support to 1.4 after support.  
• The share that reported no barriers increased from 8% to 25%.  
• All reported barrier types, including qualifications, job availability, transport, internet 
access, housing and caring responsibilities, reduced after support. 
Addressing barriers was associated with stronger employment outcomes. More than 
half of participants who reported no remaining barriers after support were in employment, 
compared with 28% of those who still reported at least 1 barrier. Participants who no 
longer saw qualifications as a barrier were also more likely than average to be in work or 
to have gained a qualification. 
Second, support contributed to soft skill development:  
• Econometric analysis found a statistically significant association between soft skill 
development and moves into employment, where, on average, a one-point increase 
in respondents’ soft skills was found to be associated with a 6% higher likelihood of 
moving into employment.  
• Qualitative evidence also identified confidence, employability and job search skills 
as important routes through which support helped participants act on opportunities.  
• Among participants who entered employment, 71% saw an increase in at least one 
soft skill. 
Soft skill gains were not always sufficient to secure employment within the 
evaluation period. Around one in five participants improved their soft skills but did not 
enter work during the observed period. This is consistent with the theory of change: for 
some participants, confidence and skills are necessary early steps before employment 
becomes realistic. 
 
 
8 This includes those who had incomplete skills data along with no other positive outcomes. 1% saw no change in average soft skills. 

 
34 
 
Qualitative evidence also supported the importance of intermediate outcomes. 
Frontline staff explained: 
“We have absolutely had lots of successes where participants have gone into the 
[project] and come out and are now in employment [or] doing qualifications. Lots 
have just done the six months [in their placement] but learned valuable skills that 
have moved them on to other employment.” (Frontline staff) 
However, the reverse was also true for some participants. While not reflective of the 
average experience, some participants who started with multiple barriers and low soft skills 
still moved into employment within the evaluation period. This reinforces the importance of 
tailored support: starting further from work reduced the likelihood of immediate 
employment on average but did not prevent substantial progress where support was able 
to address the right combination of confidence, practical skills and barriers. 
The delivery model explains why these routes were possible. Trusted one-to-one 
relationships enabled advisors to understand individual circumstances, tailor support, 
sequence activities appropriately and sustain engagement. UKSPF flexibility also allowed 
projects to respond to practical barriers, including through local delivery, discretionary 
support and referrals to specialist provision. 
Local delivery also mattered. One delivery partner explained: 
“The guys [advisors] are out and about in communities. They’re not based in any 
centres. They’ll meet people sometimes at their homes. They’ll meet people in food 
banks that are community centres, libraries, etc. It’s about really making the support 
and the programme as accessible as possible to the participants.” (Delivery partner) 
The following two case studies provide illustrative examples, drawn from the experience of 
real participants, of beneficiaries moving closer to work through personalised support.

Other factors influencing outcomes 
Other factors, including local labour market conditions, other support and changes 
in personal circumstances, may have influenced outcomes. The evaluation also did 
not include a comparison group. These limitations mean that the evidence should not be 
interpreted as proving that all outcomes were caused solely by UKSPF support. 
Progress was also harder for some groups. Participants with persistent health, disability, 
housing or multiple unresolved barriers were less likely to move quickly into employment, 
and some continued to report barriers after support. This does not undermine the overall 
contribution claim, but it shows that personalised employability support cannot fully offset 
wider structural, health or housing constraints within a short evaluation period. 

 
36 
 
However, several factors support the contribution claim. Participants often faced 
complex and connected barriers. Delivery partners and local authorities reported limited 
availability of comparable support. Available contextual evidence does not suggest that 
unusually favourable local labour markets explain the scale of observed outcomes. The 
qualitative evidence also consistently links outcomes to the personalised support model. 
Evaluation of European Social Fund (ESF) precursor programmes of support found causal 
evidence of increases in employment. ESF evaluation is not directly comparable as it 
counts additional days of employment due to the support and includes participants closer 
to employment as participants could be unemployed or employed as well as economically 
inactive. Nevertheless, it shows that broadly similar employability programmes can move 
people into employment.9 
Overall assessment of contribution 
High-strength evidence suggests that personalised support contributed to reduced 
reported barriers, improved relevant skills and helped many long-term inactive participants 
convert readiness into active job search or employment. This combines quantitative 
before-and-after survey data, self-reported impacts, econometric analysis and qualitative 
evidence from local authorities, delivery partners and participants for how the personalised 
support enabled this.  
The evidence is strongest at the overall cohort level because it combines consistent 
survey findings, qualitative evidence and clear associations between reduced barriers, 
improved skills and employment-related outcomes. 
2.2.7: Contribution claim 7: UKSPF support contributed to improvements in 
wellbeing across all cohorts  
This claim considers wellbeing outcomes across participants. It should be interpreted 
differently from the employment and barrier claims because the survey did not include a 
dedicated quantitative wellbeing measure. This was a trade-off to balance the burden of 
questions on respondents and the priorities of the evaluation. At the time of the survey 
design, wellbeing outcomes were not understood to be priority outcomes and questions on 
soft skills, barriers, perception of impact of the support and employability outcomes were 
prioritised. This limits the ability to estimate the scale or persistence of wellbeing change, 
but the consistency of evidence across participants, delivery partners and local authorities 
supports the conclusion that wellbeing improvements were an important part of the 
programme’s contribution. 
All projects saw improvements in wellbeing across their participants. Qualitative 
evidence consistently reported improvements in confidence, emotional wellbeing and 
stability. Reported outcomes included improved self-worth, reduced anxiety, greater 
independence, better engagement with services, improved family relationships and greater 
resilience. 
For some participants, wellbeing improvement was an outcome in its own right. For 
others, it was also an enabler of progress towards employment or training. 
Participants who experienced mental health challenges, housing instability, financial stress 
 
 
9 Impact evaluation of the European Social Fund 2014-2020 programme in England - GOV.UK 

 
37 
 
or domestic abuse often needed to stabilise their circumstances before they could engage 
meaningfully with employability support. 
This matters for policy because, for participants with complex needs, wellbeing and 
stability were not separate from employability. They were often preconditions for 
engaging with training, job search or work. 
How support contributed to change 
Support contributed to wellbeing through trusted relationships, holistic support and 
links to wider services. Advisors did not need to deliver all specialist support directly. 
Their role was often to build trust, understand the participant’s circumstances, help them 
navigate services and advocate for or accompany them where needed. 
This was reflected in delivery partner evidence: 
“It’s not just about getting people into work. It’s about the whole story from 
beginning to end and seeing that confidence building as well.” (Delivery partner) 
External services clearly contributed to some wellbeing outcomes, particularly where 
specialist provision addressed health, housing, debt or domestic abuse-related needs. 
However, UKSPF support often played the enabling role by helping participants access, 
coordinate and sustain engagement with those services. 
One member of frontline delivery staff explained their role in helping participants access 
external services: 
“We’ve got them [clients] in touch with social workers, we’ve got them in touch with 
their GP, we’ve got them in touch with the housing benefits organisations and all 
that kind of stuff. In some clients lives we’re the only person who has that ability to 
connect them to different people. And if we were to go, they’d lose their one point of 
contact with the rest of the world. A lot of the time they don’t have the ability to pick 
themselves up, so a lot of us have to do the picking up for them. We pick them up, 
we bring them along to the appointment, we advise them when necessary.” 
(Frontline staff) 
For participants who faced mental health challenges, housing anxiety, domestic abuse, 
debt or difficulty engaging with services, consistent advocacy helped stabilise 
circumstances, reduce anxiety and increase independence. These outcomes then made it 
more realistic for participants to consider employment, education or training. 
The following two case studies provide illustrative examples, drawn from the experience of 
real participants, of the increased wellbeing of beneficiaries following support received.

Other factors influencing outcomes 
External services and changes in individual circumstances may have influenced 
wellbeing outcomes. These should not be treated only as alternative explanations. In 
many cases, they were part of the mechanism through which UKSPF support contributed 
to change because advisors helped participants access services they may otherwise not 
have used effectively. 
The lack of a dedicated wellbeing measure means that the evaluation cannot quantify 
wellbeing change. The evidence is therefore strongest on the existence and nature of 
wellbeing improvements, rather than their scale or persistence. 

 
39 
 
Overall assessment of contribution 
Medium-strength evidence that the personalisation and holistic approach contributed to 
improving wellbeing outcomes for participants across all cohorts. The evidence is strong 
and consistent qualitatively, but the rating remains medium because wellbeing was not 
directly measured in the survey and because external services also contributed to some 
outcomes. 
2.3: Delivering value for money  
Support for economically inactive people is likely to have delivered medium VfM, 
based on indicative estimates, with high VfM expected under reasonable 
assumptions. 
The impact evaluation shows that projects met their objectives of moving people closer to 
and into employment within the timeframe of this evaluation. As well as the labour market 
(wage) benefits, employment is associated with wellbeing impacts. These outcomes are 
monetised to understand the VfM associated with the projects to date (see ‘UKSPF 
intervention-level evaluation final technical annex: support for people and skills’). 
The observed outcomes suggest a BCR of 1.1 when the employment benefits for only 
those already in employment are monetised, which is “acceptable” VfM. 
The BCR increases to 1.3 (“medium” VfM) when the monetisation also assumes that those 
who were closer to (but not in) employment within the timeframe of the evaluation actually 
move into employment within two to five years. 
Separately, including the wellbeing benefits associated with employment raises the BCR to 
1.8 (also “medium” VfM). 
These do not include wider benefits that could not yet be quantified or monetised such as:  
• increased tax receipts; 
• decreased welfare payments; 
• reduced social isolation; and  
• increased future employability through soft skill development on its own leading to 
employment.   
These non-monetised benefits are likely to materially impact the VfM assessment. It 
should also be noted that these benefits are for economically inactive people who are a 
key target group for government. Often these groups are hard to reach and disengaged. 
High VfM requires a BCR of greater than 2. Relatively small changes in assumptions 
would increase VfM to lie within this range. For instance, an assumption that employment 
lasts two years on average following support, rather than 1.5 years, increases the BCR 
from 1.1 to 2.5 (see ‘UKSPF intervention-level evaluation final technical annex: support for 
people and skills’). 

 
40 
 
Chapter 3: Process evaluation findings on 
design and delivery 
Beyond the delivery elements already outlined, two further process evaluation themes 
emerged. All process findings drew on interviews and focus groups with local authority 
leads, delivery partners, frontline delivery staff and participants, as well as reviews of 
monitoring data. These were informed by the process map set out in the Feasibility Report.  
3.1: It was essential to leverage prior experience of design 
and implementation 
All People & Skills projects in the evaluation had previously existed in some form under 
ESF provision. While eligibility criteria were typically narrowed to align with UKSPF 
objectives, project designs largely mirrored earlier ESF-funded activity. Local authorities 
and delivery partners reported that projects had been refined over several years, with 
iterative improvements made as learning accumulated. UKSPF funding enabled local 
authorities to continue interventions viewed as crucial for local economic inclusion and 
growth. 
Prior experience delivering similar projects was considered essential for effective design, 
smooth implementation and rapid mobilisation. Established frameworks, processes and 
partnerships, particularly with voluntary, community and social enterprises, helped teams 
navigate delays and uncertainties. Experience from previous project iterations was also 
important for smooth delivery. Local authorities and delivery partners relied heavily on prior 
experience to make delivery as efficient as possible and compress set-up times. Many 
commented that timelines would have been further constrained if processes needed to be 
designed from scratch. 
Planning and delivery timelines were nevertheless consistently described as constraining. 
Funding delays further compressed delivery windows, leading to rushed decision-making 
and challenges with recruiting and retaining staff. Limited time for consultation, testing or 
commissioning new providers constrained innovation; only minor adjustments to previous 
models were feasible. 
3.2: Monitoring and evaluation was less burdensome but 
missed key elements 
Monitoring requirements were lighter than under ESF, with fewer data points and less 
detail required. However, the administrative burden on local authorities and delivery 
partners was increased by unclear guidance in the early stages and initial issues with 
monitoring tools.  
Many local authorities and delivery partners felt that quantitative data alone did not fully 
capture project impact, particularly progress made by individuals who had not yet moved 
into employment. They expressed a preference to include qualitative data, such as case 

 
41 
 
studies, in submissions to MHCLG to reflect individual journeys and outcomes more 
accurately. 
Local authorities and delivery partners found it particularly helpful to measure participant 
progression by rating participants, or getting participants to rate themselves, on relevant 
soft skills at the beginning of their engagement and again at the end of their support. Many 
also measured soft skills at interim points during delivery so that progress could be 
effectively tracked and additional support could be given to individual participants where 
necessary. 
 
 

 
42 
 
Chapter 4: Implications and lessons 
4.1: Implications for policy makers 
The evaluation highlights several considerations for policy makers when interpreting these 
findings and applying them to future programme design:  
• The evidence consistently points to the role of trusted, one-to-one 
relationships between participants and advisors as a central feature associated 
with positive outcomes for inactive individuals. Delivery models that enabled 
advisors to exercise judgement, build sustained relationships, tailor support to 
individual circumstances and signpost to other services appear to underpin the 
effectiveness of these interventions.  
• Funding flexibility, including the ability of advisors to use budgets to address 
practical barriers such as transport, was regarded as key to success. Local 
partnerships with specialist delivery partners were also a critical component, 
enabling projects to address a wide range of barriers to employment concurrently.  
• Longer funding periods would allow for continuity of provision and individual 
members of delivery staff to be consistently employed. The skills of these staff 
were seen as key to successful delivery. 
• Supporting inactive individuals with a range of needs in this way can be done 
in a personalised way and offer VfM. The evaluation finds that, even under 
conservative assumptions and within a short observation window, the monetised 
benefits are expected to exceed programme costs, with additional benefits likely to 
materialise over time.  
• Schemes would never be expected to move all supported individuals into 
employment, but this is not required to deliver VfM. Intermediate outcomes 
such as reduced barriers and improved soft skills appear to represent meaningful 
benefits in their own right. For example, projects included individuals who as a 
result of support received were able to leave the house for the first time in years or 
were more able to participate actively in society and so could be better neighbours, 
family members and residents of communities.  
 
4.2: Lessons for evaluators 
Future evaluations could benefit from applying the study group approach used for this 
evaluation. It balances deep learnings from research with individual projects and grouping 
together to increase available information and the potential for robust findings. The 
evaluation and reports are designed to make the approach replicable (see detail in the 
‘UKSPF intervention-level evaluation final technical annex: support for people and skills’).  
Future evaluations could also be improved in the following ways: 

 
43 
 
• Having multiple follow-ups after the support has finished over a longer period would 
provide a better indication of longer-term employment impacts, such as whether 
employment is sustained and if more participants enter employment in a longer 
period (for instance, after completing further studies). Evaluation timelines meant 
there was only a short period of around a month before the follow-up. 
• Reliable trend data from multiple follow-ups would strengthen future analysis and 
VfM assessment by making it easier to understand whether, and at what pace, 
outcomes are sustained, increase or fade after support. It would also generate more 
data which could make quasi-experimental approaches more feasible, especially 
where suitable comparison data can also be identified.  
• This longer evaluation period could provide an opportunity for matching to similar 
individuals using HMRC data to provide a comparison group for quasi-experimental 
analysis. A longer time frame is needed for the employment and salary outcomes to 
be visible in HMRC data. Challenges would remain on understanding whether these 
matched groups had any time of employability support.  
o Alternatively, the project designs could be adapted to capture information on 
local people who could have support but did not. This could be difficult to do 
in practice and there may be innate differences between those who ask for 
support and those who do not.  
• Capturing wellbeing quantitatively in surveys could provide more specific and robust 
measures of changes to wellbeing. While trade-offs are needed in surveys to not 
overburden respondents, this evaluation has shown that further research could 
strengthen the contribution claim and more could be learned about the follow-on 
effects from improving wellbeing. 
The same survey questions could be used in the future to compare outcomes from similar 
interventions. This would increase understanding of what is working and under what 
conditions.
